questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Banisters?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Barandillas” = banisters. Origin: Spanish barandilla “railing”, from baranda. The same term is also used for: balusters.

questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Balusters?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Barandilla / Barandillas” = balusters. Origin: Spanish barandilla “railing”, from baranda. The same term is also used for: banisters.

questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Closed stringer?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Madre de Eskalera / Escalera” = closed stringer. Madre is Spanish “mother”: the main member that carries the steps, like a mother carrying her children. Escalera is Spanish “stair, ladder”.

questions.q: In Philippine construction vernacular, Quarter round is called:
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Media Cana” = quarter round. Origin: Spanish media caña “half cane”. The moulding has the rounded profile of a cut reed.

questions.q: In Philippine construction vernacular, Astragal is called:
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Batidura” = astragal. Likely from Spanish batir “to beat, strike”, the strip a door strikes against. Don't confuse Batidura (astragal, fillet) with Batidora (door fillet). The same term is also used for: fillet.

questions.q: In Philippine construction vernacular, Newel post is called:
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Tukod” = newel post. Origin: Tagalog tukod “post, prop, stake”.

questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Fillet?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Batidura” = fillet. Likely from Spanish batir “to beat, strike”, the strip a door strikes against. Don't confuse Batidura (fillet, astragal) with Batidora (door fillet). The same term is also used for: astragal.

questions.q: Which vernacular term corresponds to Riser?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Senepa, Takip Silipan” = riser. Origin: senepa is Spanish cenefa “trim, border”; takip silipan is Tagalog “covers the gap”. A riser covers the gap between treads. The same term is also used for: fascia board, plank board, skirt.

questions.q: Which vernacular term corresponds to Open stringer?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Hardinera” = open stringer. Borrowed from Spanish jardinera (Philippine Spanish hardinera), “garden planter”. How it came to mean an open stringer isn't clear. Memory hook: an open stair is airy like a garden.

questions.q: In Philippine construction vernacular, Handrail is called:
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Gabay” = handrail. Origin: Tagalog gabay “guide”. A handrail guides you up the stairs.
